225	 * this host, not an empirically measured figure (no real order was placed
226	 * to time one for this change) — the timeout/interval are named exports so
227	 * they can be retuned in one place once real timings are observed.
228	 */
229	export const GAME_PORT_CHECK_TIMEOUT_MS = 300_000;
230	export const GAME_PORT_CHECK_INTERVAL_MS = 10_000;
231	
232	/**
233	 * The 300s above is right for most of the catalog and hopeless for the rest.
234	 * First real measurements, from the 2026-09-06 whole-catalog sweep (the
235	 * "once real timings are observed" the comment above asked for):
236	 *
237	 *   minecraft 222s · palworld ~285s · rust ~310s · terraria 451s · valheim 456s
238	 *   ark       FAILS — 22.9 GB SteamCMD download, ~30 min before it binds a port
239	 *   cs2       FAILS — 71 GB download, over an hour (and needs a bigger disk)
240	 *
241	 * Terraria and Valheim already spend ~170-180s of the 300s budget inside the
242	 * game step, so the margin was thin even where it passed, and every large
243	 * Steam-based family fails outright — a HEALTHY server declared failed, which
244	 * is the same "the system asserting something untrue" class this whole health
245	 * check exists to prevent, just inverted.
246	 *
247	 * Raising the constant alone trades one wrong answer for another: a genuinely
248	 * dead server (the Terraria interactive-prompt bug) would keep a customer
249	 * waiting the whole time before failing. So instead, once the 300s check has
250	 * failed, provisioning asks the guest whether it is still WORKING — see
251	 * `waitOutGameInstall` in worker/index.ts. These bound that.
252	 *
253	 * `GAME_INSTALL_MAX_WAIT_MS` is a hard ceiling regardless of progress, sized
254	 * to cover ark comfortably; cs2 exceeds it and is blocked on disk sizing
255	 * anyway (see docs/DOCUMENTATION.md).
256	 */
257	export const GAME_INSTALL_MAX_WAIT_MS = 45 * 60_000;
258	/** One progress sample per minute — also the port-recheck window between samples. */
259	export const GAME_INSTALL_SAMPLE_MS = 60_000;
260	/** Disk growth under this between two samples does not count as progress (KB). */
261	export const GAME_INSTALL_MIN_GROWTH_KB = 8 * 1024;
262	/** Consecutive no-progress samples before giving up. */
263	export const GAME_INSTALL_STALL_LIMIT = 3;
264	/**
265	 * Restarts of the game's own systemd unit, accumulated DURING the extended
266	 * wait, that mean "crash loop" rather than "still installing".
267	 *
268	 * Why: `installProgressed` treats any container output inside the sample
269	 * window as work in progress — and a container that dies and is restarted by
270	 * systemd every few seconds produces output continuously, forever. So a
271	 * genuinely broken family never trips the stall detector and burns the entire
272	 * `GAME_INSTALL_MAX_WAIT_MS` ceiling on every one of its three attempts.
273	 * Measured on the families this catalog sweep found broken: Eco (caught at
274	 * NRestarts=30), Garry's Mod (61), The Forest (19 within nine minutes) — each
275	 * one made a customer watch "Installing the game…" for ~2.25 hours before
276	 * being told it failed, when the guest knew inside a minute.
277	 *
278	 * The generated unit (`wrapDockerGameService`) is `Restart=always`
279	 * `RestartSec=5`, and a healthy install never exits at all, so NRestarts stays
280	 * 0 for every family that works. Counting the DELTA since the wait began — not
281	 * the absolute value — keeps a container that legitimately restarted once or
282	 * twice during earlier setup from being judged on that history.
283	 */
284	export const GAME_INSTALL_RESTART_LIMIT = 3;
285	
286	/**
287	 * Has the game's systemd unit restarted enough times DURING the extended wait
288	 * to call it a crash loop? A negative reading means "unknown" (no unit, or the
289	 * guest could not be asked) and is never treated as a crash — this check can
290	 * only ever end a wait early on positive evidence.
291	 */
292	export function gameUnitCrashLooping(firstRestarts: number, currentRestarts: number): boolean {
293	  if (!Number.isFinite(firstRestarts) || !Number.isFinite(currentRestarts)) return false;
294	  if (firstRestarts < 0 || currentRestarts < 0) return false;
295	  return currentRestarts - firstRestarts >= GAME_INSTALL_RESTART_LIMIT;
296	}
297	
298	/** One reading of "is the guest still doing install work?" — see `installProgressed`. */
299	export type InstallSample = {
300	  usedKb: number;
301	  logBytes: number;
302	  /**
303	   * Cumulative CPU time (µs) the game container's cgroup has used
304	   * (`cpu.stat usage_usec`), or -1/undefined when it could not be read.
305	   */
306	  cpuUsec?: number;
307	};
308	
309	/**
310	 * Container CPU time between two samples (one GAME_INSTALL_SAMPLE_MS window)
311	 * that counts as "still working": 15 s of CPU per 60 s window, i.e. a quarter
312	 * of a core on average. An idle-but-listening game server sits far below this;
313	 * a Steam/Unreal/Unity server cooking shaders, generating a world or loading
314	 * assets sits far above it.
315	 *
316	 * Added 2026-10-01 from the live all-families sweep on node-5: Squad (21.4 GB
317	 * installed) and Stationeers (12.3 GB) both had their containers Up and the
318	 * game visibly loading, but the disk had stopped growing and neither wrote a
319	 * log line for 3 minutes — so the stall detector ended the wait as "stopped
320	 * making progress" and failed the attempt while the guest was still busy.
321	 */
322	export const GAME_INSTALL_MIN_CPU_USEC = 15_000_000;
323	
324	/**
325	 * Did the guest do any install work between two samples?
326	 *
327	 * Deliberately family-agnostic, so there is no per-image table to drift: either
328	 * the root filesystem grew by a real amount (a download or extract is running),
329	 * or the game container wrote to its log inside the sample window (world
330	 * generation, engine startup — work that need not move the disk much). Either
331	 * one counts; only both being absent means "stopped".
332	 */
333	export function installProgressed(prev: InstallSample, next: InstallSample): boolean {
334	  if (next.usedKb - prev.usedKb >= GAME_INSTALL_MIN_GROWTH_KB || next.logBytes > 0) return true;
335	  // Third signal: the container is burning CPU (asset load, world gen, shader
336	  // compile) even though it is silent and the disk is flat. Unknown readings
337	  // (-1/undefined, or a counter that went BACKWARDS because the container was
338	  // recreated) never count as progress.
339	  const a = prev.cpuUsec ?? -1;
340	  const b = next.cpuUsec ?? -1;
341	  return a >= 0 && b >= a && b - a >= GAME_INSTALL_MIN_CPU_USEC;
342	}
343	
344	/**
345	 * Real TCP-or-UDP connect check (per `GAME_PORT`'s `protocol`) against the
346	 * server's own address at the game's actual listen port — see
347	 * `gamePortForServer`. Reuses the caller's already-computed `ip` (the
348	 * dedicated public IP, or the NAT server's private address) rather than
349	 * recomputing it.
350	 *
351	 * NOTE on NAT servers: only SSH gets an automatic port-forward at provision
352	 * time (`syncPortForwardsBestEffort`); the game's own port is forwarded only
353	 * if the customer adds a `PortForward` for it (lib/actions-server.ts) — a
354	 * separate, pre-existing product gap this task does not touch. Checking
355	 * against the VM's own address (not the public NAT address) still verifies
356	 * the thing this check exists to catch — the game process itself bound the
357	 * port — independent of whether that port is yet forwarded to the internet.
358	 */
359	export async function checkGamePortOpen(
360	  host: string,
361	  port: number,
362	  protocol: "tcp" | "udp",
363	  opts?: {
364	    timeoutMs?: number;
365	    intervalMs?: number;
366	    sleep?: (ms: number) => Promise<void>;
367	    /**
368	     * Positive confirmation that the game really is bound to the port, read
369	     * from inside the guest — see `procNetHasPort` and the UDP note above.
370	     * `true` = bound, `false` = definitely not bound, `null` = could not tell
371	     * (never held against the server). Required to make the UDP path mean
372	     * anything; harmless and still useful as a second opinion for TCP.
373	     */
374	    verifyBound?: () => Promise<boolean | null>;
375	  }
376	): Promise<RetryResult> {
377	  const attempt: CheckOnce =
378	    protocol === "tcp"
379	      ? () => tcpAttempt(host, port, { timeoutMs: TCP_ATTEMPT_TIMEOUT_MS, expectSshBanner: false })
380	      : () => udpAttempt(host, port, { timeoutMs: TCP_ATTEMPT_TIMEOUT_MS });
381	  const verify = opts?.verifyBound;
382	  const checkOnce: CheckOnce = verify
383	    ? async () => {
384	        const r = await attempt();
385	        if (!r.ok) return r;
386	        const bound = await verify();
387	        if (boundVerdictPasses(protocol, bound)) return r;
388	        return {
389	          ok: false,
390	          error:
391	            bound === false
392	              ? `the ${port}/${protocol} probe drew no refusal, but nothing inside the guest is bound to ` +
393	                `${port}/${protocol} — silence is not the game listening`
394	              : `the ${port}/udp probe drew no refusal, but the guest could not confirm anything is bound ` +
395	                `to ${port}/udp — for UDP that is no evidence at all, not a pass`,
396	        };
397	      }
398	    : attempt;
399	  return retryCheck(checkOnce, {
400	    timeoutMs: opts?.timeoutMs ?? GAME_PORT_CHECK_TIMEOUT_MS,
401	    intervalMs: opts?.intervalMs ?? GAME_PORT_CHECK_INTERVAL_MS,
402	    sleep: opts?.sleep,
403	  });
404	}
405	
406	/**
407	 * Is a socket bound to `port` present in a `/proc/net/{udp,udp6,tcp,tcp6}`
408	 * table? Pure parser over the raw table text so it is unit-testable; the
409	 * caller concatenates the guest's own tables plus each running container's
410	 * (`/proc/<pid>/net/...`), because a containerised game binds the port in its
411	 * OWN network namespace, not the guest's.
412	 *
413	 * WHY THIS EXISTS: `udpAttempt` resolves SUCCESS on timeout — for a
414	 * connectionless protocol there is nothing else a generic prober can do, since
415	 * a healthy game server has no obligation to answer a byte of nonsense. So the
416	 * UDP game-port check passed on silence, and silence is exactly what a guest
417	 * emits while a crash-looping container is between restarts (the packet is
418	 * dropped rather than refused). Caught live 2026-09-07: a The Forest order was
419	 * marked DONE and handed over as ready while its container had restarted 118
420	 * times, had never started the game at all ("Missing SERVER_STEAM_ACCOUNT_TOKEN
421	 * … Aborting server start"), and had nothing bound to any port. That is the
422	 * same "the system asserting something untrue" failure this whole module was
423	 * written to end, just on the protocol half nobody had checked.
424	 *
425	 * `st` is only meaningful for TCP (0A = LISTEN); UDP sockets have no listen
426	 * state, so a bound socket is all there is to find.
427	 */
428	/**
429	 * Given the in-guest binding verdict (`true` bound / `false` not bound / `null`
430	 * could not be determined), may this attempt count as the game port being open?
431	 *
432	 * The asymmetry between the protocols is the whole point. A completed TCP
433	 * connect is real evidence by itself, so the in-guest read is only a second
434	 * opinion and "could not ask" costs nothing. A UDP probe that draws no refusal
435	 * is NOT evidence — `udpAttempt` reports success on silence — so without an
436	 * in-guest answer the attempt has established nothing, and letting "unknown"
437	 * pass would put the check straight back to being a no-op that any transient
438	 * SSH hiccup unlocks. Attempts repeat across the whole retry window, so a blip
439	 * costs one attempt; only a guest that stays unreachable for the entire window
440	 * fails here, and that guest has a real problem regardless.
441	 */
442	export function boundVerdictPasses(protocol: "tcp" | "udp", bound: boolean | null): boolean {
443	  if (bound === true) return true;
444	  if (bound === false) return false;
445	  return protocol === "tcp";
446	}
447	
448	export function procNetHasPort(table: string, port: number, opts?: { tcpListeningOnly?: boolean }): boolean {
449	  if (!Number.isInteger(port) || port <= 0 || port > 65535) return false;
450	  const want = port.toString(16).toUpperCase().padStart(4, "0");
451	  for (const line of table.split("\n")) {
452	    const f = line.trim().split(/\s+/);
453	    // sl local_address rem_address st ...
454	    if (f.length < 4 || !f[1]?.includes(":")) continue;
455	    const local = f[1];
456	    const cut = local.lastIndexOf(":");
457	    if (local.slice(cut + 1).toUpperCase() !== want) continue;
458	    if (opts?.tcpListeningOnly && f[3] !== "0A") continue;
459	    // A socket bound to loopback INSIDE the container is bound to a network

473	 *  127.0.0.1 appears as `0100007F`. */
474	function isLoopbackAddrHex(addr: string): boolean {
475	  const up = addr.toUpperCase();
476	  if (up.length === 8) return up.slice(6, 8) === "7F";
477	  if (up.length === 32) {
478	    if (up === "00000000000000000000000001000000") return true; // ::1
479	    if (up.startsWith("0000000000000000FFFF0000")) return isLoopbackAddrHex(up.slice(24)); // ::ffff:127.x.x.x

496	 * guest's own only when no container is running. The fallback order matters

498	 * guest's ROOT namespace for as long as the container is up, whether or not

500	 * showed `0.0.0.0:27015` bound while the game had never started. Counting the

527	 * healthy server into a falsely-failed check.

533	): Promise<boolean | null> {

535	  try {

537	      const r = await exec(
538	        conn,
539	        // `docker ps` failing and `docker ps` finding nothing look identical in

541	        // could not be asked must read as UNKNOWN, never as "no containers, so
542	        // look in the root namespace" — where docker-proxy would answer for a
543	        // dead game.
544	        `if ids=$(docker ps -q 2>/dev/null); then dok=1; else dok=0; fi; ` +
545	          `files=""; ` +

547	          `case "${"$"}pid" in ''|0) continue;; esac; ` +
548	          `files="${"$"}files /proc/${"$"}pid/net/${base} /proc/${"$"}pid/net/${base}6"; done; ` +

That reminds me the PASSWORD_RESET job fired at 01:50, meaning the main thread hit a failure too. So the guest's actual password diverges from what I expect. Could cloud-init's `chpasswd` config have set the password as expired, triggering a PAM password-change prompt that ssh2 would misinterpret as an auth failure? Proxmox normally sets expire to False, but I should check whether vendor data overrides that. Since Project Zomboid on node-5 works fine, I'm now comparing node-2 and node-5's setup—differing PVE versions or templates might explain the discrepancy.

Since I can't inspect the node-2 template directly, I'll document the open question with concrete diagnostic steps for the main thread: checking shadow file change dates, SSH auth failure reasons in journalctl, and cloud-init's password-setting logs. The fix I'm recommending is a credential self-heal mechanism that resets the password via QGA on any auth failure, which covers the root cause regardless of what it turns out to be—plus reusing the management key instead of rotating it each attempt, since rotation without delivery is clearly a bug.

Turning to the killed docker pull, I'm wondering if a guest reboot around 01:23:32 could explain it, since dockerd shutting down during a pull would log cleanup failures consistent with what I'm seeing.

But then I trace through the setup script's structure and realize the `&&` chain only wraps the docker install and create commands—the systemd unit file heredoc and enable/start commands run unconditionally afterward. Since the valheim unit actually got created with a restart counter, that means the script kept running past the failed docker create, which rules out a reboot or script kill as the cause—the docker create command itself failed partway through the pull after about 52 seconds, and now I need to figure out why.

Network issues from the registry seem likely—a dropped connection or TLS timeout mid-pull—and Docker Hub's anonymous rate limiting is a strong suspect, especially since node-2 shares a single public IP across all its VMs via NAT, meaning every pull from any VM on that node counts against the same shared limit. A straight rate-limit error would show up as "toomanyrequests" on the manifest fetch though, not a mid-extraction failure, so this points more toward a dropped connection during blob download.

This matches the evidence: the implicit pull inside `docker create` has zero retry logic, so any transient network blip is fatal to provisioning, yet the setup script still proceeds to install the systemd unit — which then crash-loops every 5 seconds forever because the container was never actually created, racking up a restart count in the 80s with "No such container" errors that the worker has no way to distinguish from other failure modes.

The brief's SSH-timeout theory doesn't hold up — no worker SSH session executes the pull, and the unit file's existence proves cloud-init's runcmd survived past the failed create. The real culprit is the health probe itself swallowing an authentication failure and reporting a generic "guest stopped answering," masking the actual root cause.

Now I'm trying to figure out why password auth failed on Valheim specifically, since PZ used the same code path successfully. The retry regenerated sshkeys and cipassword, and a PASSWORD_RESET via QGA ran afterward, but that doesn't confirm whether the first provisioning attempt's password actually worked — the probe's missing management key combined with the port assignment for the Valheim game service might be where things diverge.

I'm checking whether node-2's OS template differs from other nodes (different Ubuntu version, different OpenSSH config) and whether the connection logic has special per-node behavior like a guestSshPort override that could be misrouting the SSH probe for this particular server.

New verified root cause for the failed Valheim provision: duplicate private IPs on node-2. VM configs 101 (sausaugepro, running), 137, 138 and 644 all carry ip=10.20.1.101, and 106 is duplicated as well. IPAM (lib/ipam.ts allocateIp) only checks the DB, so it handed 644 an address already held by orphan or duplicate VMs. NAT then forwarded 20042 to VM 101 (ARP resolves .101 to VM 101's MAC), so the platform's SSH landed on the wrong VM.

Please add these fixes to your branch, along with the pull-timeout, credential-rotation and blank-ADMIN_USERNAME fixes:
1. allocateIp must reject any IP that appears in the DB, in any Proxmox VM config on that node (ipconfig0 and net0 across /etc/pve/qemu-server, via the node API or node-agent), or in live ARP. Fail loudly instead of reusing it.
2. provision() must verify that the guest it reaches over SSH has the expected hostname or machine-id before running any setup. On mismatch, abort with a clear error and never touch the other VM.
3. Add a startup or sweep check that flags duplicate IPs across the fleet.
4. Never touch customer VMs: the existing duplicates (101/137/138/106) are an owner decision, so only report them.

Add tests, update docs/DOCUMENTATION.md, and keep to your worktree.

I'm checking whether the game setup needs to stay as a separate file at /root/nxeon-game-setup.sh, since the worker reconcile path uploads it fresh via stdin anyway—but the cloud-init path could just keep the game logic inline within nxeon-setup.sh, so I need to verify the pgrep pattern still matches correctly either way.

The reasoning for switching to systemd-run is to isolate the process from cloud-init's cgroup lifecycle and gain systemctl/journal visibility, so now I'm double-checking the YAML scalar doesn't break due to the embedded quotes and colons in the command.

Moving on to the worker side, I'm sketching a provision-guest module with injectable shell execution types for exec and execInput, plus a connector or withGuest wrapper to abstract guest access. I'm designing an ensureGuestAccess function that takes dependencies like withGuest, a repair-via-agent fallback, and an auth-error predicate, starting with a simple liveness check via running `true` in the guest shell.

Then on failure I check if it's an auth error, attempt repair by resetting the password through the QEMU guest agent, and retry the shell check — returning structured ok/repaired/reason results that explain if credentials were rejected even after repair, hinting at a possible duplicate IP conflict. After password access is restored, I also need to ensure the management SSH key is installed by appending it to authorized_keys if missing.

I'm also sketching helper functions: one to verify guest identity by running a command and checking the verdict, and another to relaunch the game setup script by writing it fresh into /root/nxeon-game-setup.sh with proper permissions.

I'm making sure the relaunch logic starts the script as a detached systemd unit or background process while checking a pgrep guard to avoid duplicate launches, then adding a sampling step to probe startup progress and parse the result before moving into the main provisioning flow.

In the provision function I'm building a server result object with the id, root password, SSH management key, port, dedicated IP, and node, plus a helper that wraps SSH connections so I can run shell commands against the guest easily. I'm thinking through the ordering issue where on first boot the SSH banner might come up before cloud-init actually applies the root password, which could cause an early access check to fail even though the guest just needs more time.

I'm reasoning through the boot sequence timing — sshd starts after cloud-init's init stage writes the SSH keys, but the root password gets set during the later config stage, so there's a window where password auth could transiently fail right after boot while the mgmt key already works. To handle this safely I want ensureGuestAccess to retry plain password attempts for up to about a minute before falling back to the QGA repair path, and reapplying the same password via QGA on first boot is harmless since it's idempotent.

I'm also worried that adding a hard auth-failure check could break previously-working provisions, like degraded-path guests where the snippet write failed but password auth via the template's static config still works, or TCP-only port checks that never relied on SSH auth succeeding. For VPS provisioning specifically, since setup happens through cloud-init rather than SSH, I'm deciding whether to still apply the identity and access checks there.

I think duplicate IPs are still a real failure case for VPS too, since a customer's SSH could land on another customer's VM, but I need to consider non-Linux templates like Windows or FreeBSD where QGA/hostname checks might not apply the same way. Since Windows already goes through an SSH reachability check, I'll apply the identity and access verification universally but need to guard the behavior for cases where QGA repair isn't available.

I'm also adding an environment variable kill-switch (NXEON_PROVISION_GUEST_CHECKS=0) so these checks can be quickly disabled if needed. For identity mismatches, I want the customer-facing error to lead with a simple explanation that their server's network address is already in use, before showing technical details. I also need to handle the retry case for game servers — if the VM already existed and was booted before, I should relaunch the game setup script with corrected config before the readiness check, since cloud-init only runs once and reconciliation is the only way to apply a fresh config on retry, but only if the container isn't already healthy with the same config.

Since the setup script is idempotent and re-running systemd commands on an already-running unit is a no-op, I can safely always relaunch on retry. One wrinkle: regenerated setup scripts produce new random secrets per build, so the config hash will differ and trigger a container recreation — but that's fine since the server isn't live yet, and already-minted admin secrets and identity defaults persist across retries without being re-minted.

For readiness checks, I'm planning to sample startup logs every few attempts and classify issues as either fatal (abort with reason and logs) or repairable (relaunch setup once, then abort if it recurs), and I want the install-waiting logic to use the same classification while tolerating a few consecutive probe failures before surfacing a real error.

I also need to let that wait-for-install logic accept an optional startup-check callback so it can be reused elsewhere, and make sure the port-probing functions pass along the encrypted SSH management key. For the management key itself, I'm deciding to reuse the existing key and root password whenever the VM already exists and has a stored key, rather than rotating it — only generating fresh credentials when there's no existing VM. Before allocating an IP during provisioning, I also want to gather the node's inventory of VMs and containers via the PVE API to check for conflicts.

For a fresh provision this inventory feeds into allocation, but for a retry where the server already has a pre-set IP, I need to detect a conflict and decide how to handle it — I don't think silently reassigning the IP is safe since the VM may have already booted with that address baked into its cloud-init network config, so I'm weighing whether to throw loudly versus attempt an automatic re-IP in that case.

Changing ipconfig0 on a retry is tricky because Proxmox derives the cloud-init instance-id from a hash of the config, so altering the network settings and rebooting would make cloud-init treat it as a brand-new instance and rerun everything — passwords, keys, runcmd — which is a heavy, risky path. For this task I'll just fail loudly with a clear reason and let the owner decide rather than attempt that automatic re-IP.

Dedicated public IPs aren't part of this check, only NAT private ones. For ARP data, I'm planning to use local `ip neigh` output for the primary worker and call a new node-agent endpoint for others, falling back to null if it's missing. I'm sketching out a node-ip-inventory module that lists VMs/containers per node, fetches each config, and gathers neighbor entries alongside any errors encountered.

If any config read fails, I want to throw rather than silently proceed, since we can't prove an IP is free otherwise — though with ~100+ VMs per provision this could mean significant latency, so a short-lived cache per node seems worth adding. I'm also thinking through a periodic fleet-wide sweep (on startup and every 6 hours) that checks each active node for duplicate IPs, logging any conflicts and cross-referencing against the database's server records.

If this inventory read fails, provisioning should fail loudly with a clear error naming the node.

Then I'm resolving the actual IP to use — either the dedicated address, the server's existing IP, or a freshly allocated one that avoids held IPs — and checking for conflicts against the inventory entries if this isn't a dedicated allocation.

If a conflict is found, I throw immediately so setup stops before anything starts, since retrying wouldn't help since the same conflict would recur. I need to make sure the conflict check properly excludes the server's own existing config and ARP entries matching its own MAC, and I should also pass `heldElsewhere` through the fallback allocation path, though I'll leave the reinstall and admin-ops fallback paths as follow-up items for now. Next I'm moving to the management key reuse logic, replacing the block that checks for an existing management public key tied to the server's vmid and SSH settings.

For reuse, if an existing management key is found I log and reuse it; otherwise I generate a new key pair and fall back gracefully if generation fails. Then, once SSH is reachable, I'm setting up a guest server object carrying the root password, SSH port, and dedicated IP info, wrapping it so guest checks can run through an SSH shell, gated behind an environment variable that lets these checks be skipped if needed.

Now I'm verifying access to the new server using ensureGuestAccess, which can reapply credentials if needed, and throwing a clear error if login fails. After that, I'm fetching the VM's config to check its SMBIOS UUID and verifying the guest's identity matches the expected hostname/UUID -- if it doesn't match, I throw an error since this would mean the IP is pointing at a different machine entirely, which is a critical safety check before handing over the server.

I'm wondering whether the hostname set by cloud-init actually matches server.hostname consistently, especially on retries or if the VM name contains unusual characters, since Proxmox derives the hostname from the VM's name field.

Then I move to checking the game reconcile step on retry, looking at how the game family, control spec service hints, docker container name, and secret values from config get pulled together to figure out what needs repairing.

For the actual retry logic, I want to compute whether the guest is already booted using the `alreadyRunning` flag established earlier rather than re-deriving it, then re-apply the fresh game setup script by relaunching against the existing guest with a regenerated build script that carries over the game config and any Minecraft jar pin.

The idea is to only sample restart counts periodically (roughly every 30 seconds) and compare against a baseline captured at the first check, so I can detect sudden restart spikes indicating crashes. I'm refining when exactly to capture that baseline — ideally right before checking if the game port is open — so that retries after a relaunch get an accurate fresh starting point rather than inheriting stale counts from before.

I'm also working through the classification logic: a fatal verdict returns a redacted error reason immediately, a repair verdict tries relaunching the setup script if repair attempts remain (decrementing the counter and resetting baseline), and otherwise returns a final failure message; wait/ok verdicts just continue polling. I need to account for edge cases like the brief window where cloud-init has finished but the setup service hasn't started writing its pid file yet, and scripts that don't match the expected container launch pattern.

I also need to think about retries: if this is a fatal config issue, retrying with the same config on the next attempt would likely just fail the same way again, unless something in the setup code corrects it first.

So I'm wondering if a fatal abort should skip remaining retry attempts entirely, which would require touching the job attempt logic in runJob — maybe throwing a special error flagged as non-retriable so the job gets marked FAILED immediately. content.thinking:
Since my scripts are read-only, I don't need extra safety guards here. For A2S queries I'm figuring out port mapping — probing TCP join ports with a connect attempt and UDP ports with A2S queryInfo, since most Source/Unity Steam servers respond on their join port (like Valheim's 2457), then mapping each guest join port to its public forwarded port.

If no UDP port answers A2S, I'll just mark it "unverified externally" rather than a failure, since the in-guest bound-port check already covers that case. For memory, I'll compare `free -m` total against the plan's RAM allowance with roughly 10% slack for kernel reservations, cross-checked against Proxmox's configured memory/balloon settings.

Laying out the verify script's read-only steps: pull server/node/plan/portForward data, check Proxmox VM status and config, scan the node's IP inventory for duplicates, then SSH in to confirm identity, startup health, container state, image digest, bound ports, memory, and disk usage — finishing with external TCP/UDP reachability checks against the forwarded public ports.

Then I'll have it print a checklist of PASS/FAIL/WARN results, exiting 0 only when everything passes, with a "clean bill of health" message on success. I want the core logic as a pure `summarizeHealth(checks)` function separate from the script's I/O, so now I'm writing scripts/verify-game-provision.ts, reusing the port-checking helpers from provision-health with a short timeout for verification.

content.thinking:
I'm thinking about whether cPanel or CyberPanel installers might alter the SSH config mid-check since those installers can run for 30+ minutes in the background, but the retry logic (4 attempts over 15s) should cover any transient failure from a sshd restart. I'm also considering whether the hostname field for a VPS reflects a customer-chosen value.

Cloud-init pulls the hostname from the Proxmox VM name, and since UUID is the primary identifier, any FQDN vs short-name mismatch shouldn't matter. I'm also checking that qemu-guest-agent is bundled in VPS templates, then thinking through retry/reconcile edge cases—if a worker restarts mid-provision and setup is still running in the guest, I should leave it alone rather than relaunch; similarly if the setup verdict shows a container missing early because of an in-progress pull, I should just wait. The trickier case is when the game portion of setup finished but the container is missing because the family script didn't match the wrap's header regex, meaning no state or pid was recorded even though `docker run -d` still created a container under a name I'd need to catch via the dockerContainerNameFrom pattern instead.

For old-style scripts without a pid file, if cloud-init reports done but the actual `docker run` is still executing under nohup/systemd-run, my verdict logic could misclassify this as needing repair and trigger a relaunch via freshGameScript, producing a duplicate "name already in use" conflict—mostly harmless since current families match the wrap pattern, but worth tightening by only treating a missing container as repairable when a state file exists. The real case where setupState is empty and the container is missing without setup running is when the node-agent snippet write failed entirely, meaning setup never started—relaunching is the correct fix there, so I'll keep that behavior. Finally, for fatal startup verdicts, I throw a ProvisionStopError so no retries occur.

I'm also considering whether a transient Docker Hub rate-limit error could masquerade as fatal: journal logs from `docker start -a` showing "No such container" plus repeated restarts match my fatal pattern, but since the missing-container case is already handled earlier via the repair branch, this shouldn't double-fire. If Docker Hub throttling causes setup to fail and the container ends up missing, repair triggers a relaunch with in-guest retries using exponential backoff up to about 225 seconds total, and if that still fails, a second repair isn't allowed, so it returns a retriable (non-fatal) error—which seems right. I also want to check whether some legitimately slow-starting games that exit after an initial install step and rely on restart policies could get wrongly classified as fatal.

My pattern-matching could be too broad: phrases like "is required" might match benign messages such as "A restart is required to apply updates," so combined with two legitimate restarts during first boot, that could trigger a false fatal. I should tighten the fatal-line patterns—dropping the overly generic "is required" match while keeping "FATAL"/"PANIC" since those genuinely indicate crashes—and reconsider whether "Error response from daemon" is specific enough to avoid false positives too.

Given that, I'll make fatal verdicts non-retriable only when a recognized crash pattern actually matches, while unpatterned 3-restart loops stay retriable since those could be transient issues like corrupted downloads or OOM. I also want the customer-facing message for a fatal failure to clearly state the game didn't stay running so it wasn't handed over as ready. Time to apply these refinements to the detection logic.

# Provisioning first-boot RCA — 2026-10-02

Two free partner-grant game servers (created through `lib/partner-grants.ts` →
`placeGameOrder`) failed PROVISION at about 01:20 UTC on 2026-10-02. Both jobs
went through all 3 attempts and ended `FAILED`. This document explains why,
using the worker journal, the `Job` and `Server` rows, the live catalog rows,
and the evidence the main thread collected on the VMs. It then lists what
changed on branch `fix/provisioning-first-boot-reliability`.

Line references marked **main** point at `main` as of commit `1d72f3d9e6` (the
code that ran). References without a marker point at this branch.

---

## A. projectzomboid-syep3t (VM 645, node-5, 8 GB / 16 players)

### What happened

| time (UTC) | evidence |
|---|---|
| 01:21:29 | PROVISION claimed |
| 01:21:41 | `minted per-server ADMIN_PASSWORD, RCON_PASSWORD (catalog default was a shared placeholder)` |
| 01:30:53 | attempt 1 fails: `game port 27015/tcp never opened … The game container is crash-looping — its service restarted 4 times in 3 minute(s) of waiting (systemd NRestarts is now 10)` |
| 01:38:30 | attempt 2 fails the same way (NRestarts 25) |
| 01:46:08 | attempt 3 fails the same way (NRestarts 39) and the job ends `FAILED` |

In the guest, the container started, validated its files, and the game exited
at once with `invalid username given to "-adminusername"`, then `Server
exited`, a NullPointerException on shutdown, and container exit code 0. The
container env had `ADMIN_USERNAME=` (empty).

### Root cause: a blank schema default overwrote the catalog's real value

1. **The PZ schema default was `""`.** `lib/game-config.ts:1263` **main**:
   `{ key: "ADMIN_USERNAME", …, default: "" }`.
2. **`validateConfig` fills every missing field with its default.**
   `lib/game-config.ts:2485` **main** (`const v = provided ? String(raw) :
   String(field.default)`), called on every order at `lib/game-order.ts:379`.
   The grant passed no config, so the persisted `Server.gameConfig` contained
   `"ADMIN_USERNAME": ""`. The row is visible in prod.
3. **`applyGameConfigEnv` substitutes any non-null value.**
   `worker/game-variant.ts:161-162` **main** skips only `undefined`/`null`.
   That turned the catalog's `-e ADMIN_USERNAME=admin` (live
   `OsTemplate.setupScript`) into `-e ADMIN_USERNAME=''`.
4. **The image passes the value straight to `-adminusername`**, and the game
   refuses to start with an empty one.

The admin *passwords* were fine. `adminSecretFieldsToMint` minted real values
because the catalog's `changeme12` is a known weak placeholder. Nothing did the
equivalent for an admin *account name*.

**Scope audit.** I compared every family's live `setupScript` (all
`OsTemplate` rows) with its schema. I listed each string field whose default is
`""` and whose env var appears in the script with a non-blank value (the
script is in the scratchpad: `provfix/audit.ts`). `projectzomboid
ADMIN_USERNAME` is the only identity-type value this pattern destroys. All the
other hits are passwords:

- **Admin/RCON passwords with catalog `changeme12`:** ARK, PZ, Icarus, KF2,
  L4D2, Soulmask, TF2, CS2 (`changeme`). `adminSecretFieldsToMint` already
  mints these.
- **Join passwords:** abioticfactor, ARK, barotrauma, nightingale, vrising. A
  blank value there means an open server, which is a valid choice, so it is
  left as it is.

Blank admin secrets with no schema field are filled per build: Palworld
`ADMIN_PASSWORD`, Rust `RUST_RCON_PASSWORD`, Arma Reforger `ADMIN_PASSWORD`,
and DayZ creds (`buildGameSetupScript`). Families that need a value the
customer must supply are already `required: true` and fail at order time, not
at provision: Valheim `SERVER_PASS`, The Forest `password`, Dragonwilds
`OWNER_ID`/`ADMIN_PASSWORD`, Sunkenland `worldGuid`, DST `TOKEN`, Mordhau
`SERVER_ADMINPW`.

### Why it took 15 minutes and 3 attempts to say so

- The base port check (`worker/provision-health.ts:229` **main**, 300 s)
  probes only the port. A game that exits on start looks exactly like one
  that is still installing.
- Crash-loop detection existed only inside the extended wait
  (`waitOutGameInstall`, `worker/index.ts:614` **main**,
  `GAME_INSTALL_RESTART_LIMIT=3`). That wait starts after the 300 s window.
- The error carried the restart count but none of the game's own words.
- `runJob` retried the identical configuration twice more
  (`worker/index.ts:2690` **main**).
- The unit is `Restart=always` / `RestartSec=5` with no backoff
  (`worker/game-variant.ts:253` **main**), so the guest restarted the game
  about every 30 s, 40+ times.

---

## B. valheim-gjjrv9 (VM 644, node-2, 8 GB / 20, vanilla)

### What happened

| time (UTC) | evidence |
|---|---|
| 01:20:17 | PROVISION claimed |
| 01:20:34 | per-VM snippet written via node-agent on node-2 |
| 01:22:25 | cloud-init finished in the guest |
| 01:22:40 | docker installed by `/root/nxeon-setup.sh`, then `docker create`'s implicit pull of `lloesche/valheim-server` started |
| 01:23:32 | dockerd: `failed to cleanup "extract-…"`: the pull was aborted |
| 01:27:40 | attempt 1 fails: `game port 2456/udp never opened … Could not check whether the install was still running (the guest stopped answering).` |
| 01:27:42 / 01:33:09 | attempts 2 and 3: `vm 644 already exists — skipping clone (idempotent retry)`, a fresh snippet is written (never applied, because cloud-init runs once per instance), and both fail identically |
| 01:50:07 | main thread's `PASSWORD_RESET` job (guest-agent path) |

Guest afterwards: `docker images` was empty, `No such container: valheim`, and
`valheim.service` had restarted 85 times. A manual `docker pull` later finished
in about 50 s.

### Root cause 1 (verified by the main thread): duplicate private IP on node-2

VM configs 101 (`sausaugepro`, running), 137, 138 and **644** all carry
`ip=10.20.1.101`, and `.106` is duplicated as well.

- **IPAM only checks the DB.** `pickFreeIp`, `lib/ipam.ts:190-210` **main**,
  reads `Server.ipAddress` plus in-flight VM moves. VM configs on the node and
  the node's ARP table are never consulted, so orphan or drifted VMs that hold
  an address with no matching DB row are invisible. `allocateIp` is called at
  `worker/index.ts:799` **main**.
- **The wrong VM answers.** NAT forwarded the server's SSH port to
  10.20.1.101. The node's ARP resolved that address to VM 101's MAC, so the
  platform's SSH reached a different customer's VM. That explains every
  symptom:
  - the install probe's login failed (`worker/index.ts:573-606` **main**). Its
    `catch {}` turned that into "the guest stopped answering", which hid the
    authentication failure.
  - attempts 2 and 3 got "All configured authentication methods failed".
  - the main thread had to reset the password via the guest agent, which
    addresses the VM by vmid and so reached the right machine.
- **The killed pull is very likely the same fault.** Two VMs answering for one
  address on one bridge means the node's ARP entry for .101 flips between two
  MACs. Long-lived TCP flows from 644 (a multi-hundred-MB layer download)
  lose their return traffic mid-stream, and an aborted layer download is
  exactly what makes dockerd log `failed to cleanup "extract-…"`. This is
  inferred, not proven from a packet trace.

**What it was not: an SSH exec timeout on the pull.** The brief suspected
`SETUP_TIMEOUT_MS = 60_000` (`lib/ssh-exec.ts:36`). PROVISION never runs the
setup or the pull over SSH. The setup is launched inside the guest by
cloud-init `runcmd` (`worker/cloud-init-parts.ts:44` **main**, `nohup
/root/nxeon-setup.sh … &`). The worker's only SSH calls during provision are
short read-only probes. The guest itself proves the script was not killed:
`valheim.service` exists, and the script only writes the unit after the
`docker create` line (`worker/game-variant.ts:264` **main**,
`${prefix}${createCmd}\n${unit}`). So the script kept running, and the
`docker create` itself failed.

### Root cause 2: nothing retries or repairs a failed pull

- **One shot, no retry.** The setup ran a single `docker create` (and so a
  single implicit pull) with no retry (`worker/game-variant.ts:238` **main**).
  When it failed, the script carried on and installed and enabled a unit
  around a container that did not exist. systemd then restarted that unit
  forever (85 times).
- **Nothing to re-run.** Cloud-init runs the snippet once per instance. A
  retry does not reboot the guest, so attempts 2 and 3 had no mechanism at all
  to re-run the setup. They waited 300 s for a port that nothing would ever
  open.

### Root cause 3: credentials rotated on retry

`provision()` minted a **new management keypair on every attempt**
(`worker/index.ts:1031` **main**), stored it, and put it in `sshkeys`
(`worker/index.ts:1044` **main**). Cloud-init installs `sshkeys` on the first
boot only, so from attempt 2 on the DB held a key the guest had never seen.

The root password was already handled correctly
(`worker/index.ts:759` **main**, fixed 2026-08-28): it is reused when a vmid
exists. The key never got the same treatment. In this incident the duplicate
IP masked the effect, but on a correctly addressed VM it still breaks every
key-based login (control panel, mods, backups) after any retried provision.

### Contributing: non-primary node first boot

- **Shared Docker Hub budget.** node-2 is a NAT island. Every VM there shares
  one public egress IP, and so one anonymous Docker Hub pull budget. Every
  provision, reinstall and sweep on that node pulls from Docker Hub directly.
  There is no mirror or cache, and game images are not pinned by digest.
- **Hidden probe errors.** `waitOutGameInstall` gave up on the first failed
  probe and discarded the error message.

---

## What changed (this branch)

### 1. IPAM knows what the node knows

- **Inventory.** `lib/node-ip-inventory.ts` reads every qemu and LXC config on
  the node. `lib/provision-guard.ts` parses `ipconfigN ip=` and LXC `netN ip=`
  plus MACs (`ipsFromVmConfig`, `macsFromVmConfig`). The live ARP table comes
  from the worker's own `ip -4 -j neigh` on the primary, or from the new
  read-only node-agent endpoint `GET /v1/net/neigh` (agent v4,
  `node-agent/index.js`) elsewhere.
- **Allocation.** `allocateIp(nodeId, serverId, { heldElsewhere })`
  (`lib/ipam.ts`) excludes every address held by another VM or answering ARP
  from a foreign MAC.
- **Retries re-prove their address.** `provision()` checks the address already
  on the row with `ipConflictReason`. A conflict throws `ProvisionStopError`,
  which fails at once, names the other VMs, and never touches them.
- **Fail loudly.** If the VM configs cannot be read, the provision stops. It
  never guesses. The emergency switch `NXEON_IP_INVENTORY=off` restores the
  old DB-only behaviour.
- **Fleet audit.** `worker/ip-audit.ts` runs at start-up and every 6 h as the
  `fleet-ip-audit` sweep. It is **report-only** and logs each finding to
  ErrorLog under `fleet.ip-audit`:
  - duplicate IPs,
  - DB rows whose IP differs from their own VM config,
  - DB rows whose IP is also configured on another VM.

  `scripts/fleet-ip-audit.ts` runs the same audit on demand.

### 2. Log in with what the guest has, and prove it is the right guest

All in `provision()`, after the SSH banner check. Helpers are in
`worker/provision-guest.ts`.

- **Login** (`ensureGuestAccess`): log in with the stored credentials only
  (management key, then password), using up to 4 plain attempts so first-boot
  cloud-init has time to finish. On an authentication failure, re-apply the
  same stored password through the QEMU guest agent (`applyPasswordToGuest`,
  addressed by vmid) and try again. If the guest still rejects it, the reason
  says the SSH address reaches a different machine (`ProvisionStopError`).
- **Identity** (`verifyGuestIdentity`): compare
  `/sys/class/dmi/id/product_uuid` with the VM config's `smbios1 uuid=`, with
  the hostname as a fallback. A mismatch stops the provision before anything
  is run or written.
- **Key install.** Only after identity passes, `installManagementKey`
  idempotently appends the stored public key (passed on STDIN).
- **No rotation.** The management key is reused once a vmid exists
  (`shouldReuseManagementKey`).

`NXEON_PROVISION_GUEST_CHECKS=0` disables this whole block.

### 3. Game setup is retried, idempotent, resumable and observable

`wrapDockerGameService` (`worker/game-variant.ts`), the single place every
family's `docker run -d` is rewritten:

- **Retried create.** `docker create` (which does the pull) is retried up to
  `CREATE_ATTEMPTS = 6` times with 15/30/45/60/75 s backoff. Layers that
  finished downloading are kept by dockerd, so a retry resumes.
- **Idempotent.** An existing container built from the same command (a
  SHA-256 prefix stored in `/var/lib/nxeon/game-container.cfg`) is kept. A
  container built from a different command, such as an earlier attempt's
  broken config, is replaced. A re-run therefore re-applies a corrected
  config.
- **Observable.** Progress and failures go to
  `/var/lib/nxeon/game-setup.state`. The setup PID is in
  `/var/lib/nxeon/game-setup.pid`, and `flock` prevents two runs overlapping.
- **Unit backoff.** The unit adds `RestartSteps=5` and `RestartMaxDelaySec=120`
  (restarts back off from 5 s to 120 s; systemd ≥ 254 is needed, older
  versions ignore the keys) and `StartLimitIntervalSec=0` (a customer's
  Start/Restart is never refused). `Restart=always` is kept on purpose: an
  in-game `/stop` that exits 0 must keep its current power semantics, which R
  owns.
- **Retried docker install.** `get.docker.com` is retried 3 times.
- **Registry mirror.** `NXEON_DOCKER_REGISTRY_MIRROR` (opt-in, validated)
  writes `daemon.json` `registry-mirrors` on a guest that has no Docker yet.

Cloud-init now starts the setup as its own transient unit
(`systemd-run --unit=nxeon-setup`, `worker/cloud-init-parts.ts`), with the old
nohup as a fallback.

### 4. Readiness uses the guest's evidence

- **Startup verdicts.** `classifyStartup` (`lib/provision-guard.ts`) takes one
  sample from `startupProbeCommand`: unit NRestarts, container state, exit
  code, last run length, setup state, whether setup is still running, and the
  unit journal, docker logs and setup log tails. It returns `wait`, `repair`
  or `fatal`.
- **When it runs.** Before the port wait, every third port attempt (about
  every 30 s, through `shouldAbort` in `retryCheck`/`checkGamePortOpen`), and
  on every extended-wait sample.
- **`fatal`** means the game exits on start: 2 restarts with a recognised
  fatal line, or 3 without one, counted from the start of the wait. The
  provision ends immediately. `Job.error`'s first line is customer-safe, and
  the following lines carry the game's own last lines with secrets redacted
  (`formatGuestLines`). With a recognised line it is a `ProvisionStopError`
  (no retry). A bare restart loop keeps the normal retry path.
- **`repair`** means no container and no setup running. The worker writes a
  fresh copy of the game setup via STDIN to `/root/nxeon-game-setup.sh` and
  launches it detached (`relaunchGameSetup`). It then keeps polling with
  short reads, once per attempt. If it is still broken, the attempt fails with
  the setup's own output.
- **Retry on a booted guest.** It always re-applies the current config through
  the setup before waiting. Cloud-init will not run again.
- **`waitOutGameInstall`** tolerates 2 failed probes, gives up on the third,
  and reports the real error.
- **No retry for deterministic failures.** `runJob` fails a `ProvisionStopError`
  immediately instead of using up the remaining attempts.

### 5. Blank identity values

- PZ `ADMIN_USERNAME` now defaults to `"admin"` (`lib/game-config.ts`).
- `applyGameConfigEnv` never substitutes a blank identity value
  (`isIdentityEnvKey`) over a non-blank catalog one.
- `provision()` persists `blankIdentityDefaults(...)` (the catalog value, or
  `"admin"`) into `gameConfig` alongside the minted secrets, so the customer
  sees the real admin user in Settings.

### 6. Self-check

`scripts/verify-game-provision.ts <serverId|hostname> [--json]` is read-only.
It checks:

- VM running,
- private IP not configured elsewhere on the node,
- identity,
- container running,
- setup state,
- recent fatal lines,
- unit active with no automatic restarts in the last 10 min,
- image and digest,
- disk,
- memory vs plan, including Proxmox memory and balloon,
- every join port bound in the guest,
- every join port reachable from outside (TCP connect, or A2S for UDP).

It exits 0 only with `CLEAN BILL OF HEALTH`.

---

## Design only: registry mirror / pull-through cache for non-primary nodes

The opt-in hook is built (`NXEON_DOCKER_REGISTRY_MIRROR`). The cache itself is
not.

1. **Where.** Run `registry:2` in proxy mode
   (`REGISTRY_PROXY_REMOTEURL=https://registry-1.docker.io`, ideally with a
   Docker Hub account token so the cache pulls with authenticated limits) on
   each node's host, listening only on the NAT bridge gateway
   (`10.20.N.1:5000`). Guests reach it without leaving the node, and the node
   pulls each layer once for all its VMs. A single cache on the primary would
   force non-primary guests across the public internet to the primary. That
   is slower than Docker Hub's CDN, so a per-node cache is preferred.
2. **How guests use it.** Set the mirror per node rather than globally: store
   it on `Node` (e.g. `Node.registryMirror`). A global env var is the stop-gap.
   Docker falls back to the upstream registry when the mirror fails, so a dead
   cache costs nothing.
3. **Pre-warm.** After a catalog image changes, pull every catalog image
   through each node's cache.
4. **Digest pinning.** The platform does not record image digests today. The
   catalog uses tags, and Minecraft is the only family with a pinned artifact
   (the jar mirror). Recording `RepoDigests` after a verified provision
   (`scripts/verify-game-provision.ts` prints it) and pinning `image@sha256:…`
   in the catalog would make every node pull the identical, cache-friendly
   image. It is not done here because it changes the catalog contract, which
   D2 owns.

## Residual risks / not verified

- **No live run.** Per this task's rules, nothing was run against a real node
  or VM. The generated setup was executed against a fake `docker` in a temp
  dir (`test/provision-first-boot.test.ts`). The SSH, guest-agent and Proxmox
  paths are tested with fakes only.
- **Proxmox token permissions.** Every provision now reads every VM config on
  its node, which needs `VM.Audit` on `/vms`. If any node's token lacks it,
  provisions on that node stop with a clear error. Check first with
  `npx tsx scripts/fleet-ip-audit.ts`: an `unreadable` line identifies the
  node.
- **ARP on non-primary nodes** needs node-agent v4, which must be redeployed
  to each node. Until then those nodes are checked against VM configs only.
  This is logged, not fatal.
- **Restart backoff** applies only to units written by new provisions and
  reinstalls. Existing servers keep their current unit.
- **Unrelated failing tests.** 17 test files fail on `main` before and after
  this change (pricing, proration, auth-lockouts and others); they are not
  related to this work.

Two free partner-grant game servers (created through `lib/partner-grants.ts` →
`placeGameOrder`) failed PROVISION at about 01:20 UTC on 2026-10-02. Both jobs
went through all 3 attempts and ended `FAILED`. This document explains why,
using the worker journal, the `Job` and `Server` rows, the live catalog rows,
and the evidence the main thread collected on the VMs. It then lists what
changed on branch `fix/provisioning-first-boot-reliability`.

Line references marked **main** point at `main` as of commit `1d72f3d9e6` (the
code that ran). References without a marker point at this branch.

---

## A. projectzomboid-syep3t (VM 645, node-5, 8 GB / 16 players)

### What happened

| time (UTC) | evidence |
|---|---|
| 01:21:29 | PROVISION claimed |
| 01:21:41 | `minted per-server ADMIN_PASSWORD, RCON_PASSWORD (catalog default was a shared placeholder)` |
| 01:30:53 | attempt 1 fails: `game port 27015/tcp never opened … The game container is crash-looping — its service restarted 4 times in 3 minute(s) of waiting (systemd NRestarts is now 10)` |
| 01:38:30 | attempt 2 fails the same way (NRestarts 25) |
| 01:46:08 | attempt 3 fails the same way (NRestarts 39) and the job ends `FAILED` |

In the guest, the container started, validated its files, and the game exited
at once with `invalid username given to "-adminusername"`, then `Server
exited`, a NullPointerException on shutdown, and container exit code 0. The
container env had `ADMIN_USERNAME=` (empty).

### Root cause: a blank schema default overwrote the catalog's real value

1. **The PZ schema default was `""`.** `lib/game-config.ts:1263` **main**:
   `{ key: "ADMIN_USERNAME", …, default: "" }`.
2. **`validateConfig` fills every missing field with its default.**
   `lib/game-config.ts:2485` **main** (`const v = provided ? String(raw) :
   String(field.default)`), called on every order at `lib/game-order.ts:379`.
   The grant passed no config, so the persisted `Server.gameConfig` contained
   `"ADMIN_USERNAME": ""`. The row is visible in prod.
3. **`applyGameConfigEnv` substitutes any non-null value.**
   `worker/game-variant.ts:161-162` **main** skips only `undefined`/`null`.
   That turned the catalog's `-e ADMIN_USERNAME=admin` (live
   `OsTemplate.setupScript`) into `-e ADMIN_USERNAME=''`.
4. **The image passes the value straight to `-adminusername`**, and the game
   refuses to start with an empty one.

The admin *passwords* were fine. `adminSecretFieldsToMint` minted real values
because the catalog's `changeme12` is a known weak placeholder. Nothing did the
equivalent for an admin *account name*.

**Scope audit.** I compared every family's live `setupScript` (all
`OsTemplate` rows) with its schema. I listed each string field whose default is
`""` and whose env var appears in the script with a non-blank value (the
script is in the scratchpad: `provfix/audit.ts`). `projectzomboid
ADMIN_USERNAME` is the only identity-type value this pattern destroys. All the
other hits are passwords:

- **Admin/RCON passwords with catalog `changeme12`:** ARK, PZ, Icarus, KF2,
  L4D2, Soulmask, TF2, CS2 (`changeme`). `adminSecretFieldsToMint` already
  mints these.
- **Join passwords:** abioticfactor, ARK, barotrauma, nightingale, vrising. A
  blank value there means an open server, which is a valid choice, so it is
  left as it is.

Blank admin secrets with no schema field are filled per build: Palworld
`ADMIN_PASSWORD`, Rust `RUST_RCON_PASSWORD`, Arma Reforger `ADMIN_PASSWORD`,
and DayZ creds (`buildGameSetupScript`). Families that need a value the
customer must supply are already `required: true` and fail at order time, not
at provision: Valheim `SERVER_PASS`, The Forest `password`, Dragonwilds
`OWNER_ID`/`ADMIN_PASSWORD`, Sunkenland `worldGuid`, DST `TOKEN`, Mordhau
`SERVER_ADMINPW`.

### Why it took 15 minutes and 3 attempts to say so

- The base port check (`worker/provision-health.ts:229` **main**, 300 s)
  probes only the port. A game that exits on start looks exactly like one
  that is still installing.
- Crash-loop detection existed only inside the extended wait
  (`waitOutGameInstall`, `worker/index.ts:614` **main**,
  `GAME_INSTALL_RESTART_LIMIT=3`). That wait starts after the 300 s window.
- The error carried the restart count but none of the game's own words.
- `runJob` retried the identical configuration twice more
  (`worker/index.ts:2690` **main**).
- The unit is `Restart=always` / `RestartSec=5` with no backoff
  (`worker/game-variant.ts:253` **main**), so the guest restarted the game
  about every 30 s, 40+ times.

---

## B. valheim-gjjrv9 (VM 644, node-2, 8 GB / 20, vanilla)

### What happened

| time (UTC) | evidence |
|---|---|
| 01:20:17 | PROVISION claimed |
| 01:20:34 | per-VM snippet written via node-agent on node-2 |
| 01:22:25 | cloud-init finished in the guest |
| 01:22:40 | docker installed by `/root/nxeon-setup.sh`, then `docker create`'s implicit pull of `lloesche/valheim-server` started |
| 01:23:32 | dockerd: `failed to cleanup "extract-…"`: the pull was aborted |
| 01:27:40 | attempt 1 fails: `game port 2456/udp never opened … Could not check whether the install was still running (the guest stopped answering).` |
| 01:27:42 / 01:33:09 | attempts 2 and 3: `vm 644 already exists — skipping clone (idempotent retry)`, a fresh snippet is written (never applied, because cloud-init runs once per instance), and both fail identically |
| 01:50:07 | main thread's `PASSWORD_RESET` job (guest-agent path) |

Guest afterwards: `docker images` was empty, `No such container: valheim`, and
`valheim.service` had restarted 85 times. A manual `docker pull` later finished
in about 50 s.

### Root cause 1 (verified by the main thread): duplicate private IP on node-2

VM configs 101 (`sausaugepro`, running), 137, 138 and **644** all carry
`ip=10.20.1.101`, and `.106` is duplicated as well.

- **IPAM only checks the DB.** `pickFreeIp`, `lib/ipam.ts:190-210` **main**,
  reads `Server.ipAddress` plus in-flight VM moves. VM configs on the node and
  the node's ARP table are never consulted, so orphan or drifted VMs that hold
  an address with no matching DB row are invisible. `allocateIp` is called at
  `worker/index.ts:799` **main**.
- **The wrong VM answers.** NAT forwarded the server's SSH port to
  10.20.1.101. The node's ARP resolved that address to VM 101's MAC, so the
  platform's SSH reached a different customer's VM. That explains every
  symptom:
  - the install probe's login failed (`worker/index.ts:573-606` **main**). Its
    `catch {}` turned that into "the guest stopped answering", which hid the
    authentication failure.
  - attempts 2 and 3 got "All configured authentication methods failed".
  - the main thread had to reset the password via the guest agent, which
    addresses the VM by vmid and so reached the right machine.
- **The killed pull is very likely the same fault.** Two VMs answering for one
  address on one bridge means the node's ARP entry for .101 flips between two
  MACs. Long-lived TCP flows from 644 (a multi-hundred-MB layer download)
  lose their return traffic mid-stream, and an aborted layer download is
  exactly what makes dockerd log `failed to cleanup "extract-…"`. This is
  inferred, not proven from a packet trace.

**What it was not: an SSH exec timeout on the pull.** The brief suspected
`SETUP_TIMEOUT_MS = 60_000` (`lib/ssh-exec.ts:36`). PROVISION never runs the
setup or the pull over SSH. The setup is launched inside the guest by
cloud-init `runcmd` (`worker/cloud-init-parts.ts:44` **main**, `nohup
/root/nxeon-setup.sh … &`). The worker's only SSH calls during provision are
short read-only probes. The guest itself proves the script was not killed:
`valheim.service` exists, and the script only writes the unit after the
`docker create` line (`worker/game-variant.ts:264` **main**,
`${prefix}${createCmd}\n${unit}`). So the script kept running, and the
`docker create` itself failed.

### Root cause 2: nothing retries or repairs a failed pull

- **One shot, no retry.** The setup ran a single `docker create` (and so a
  single implicit pull) with no retry (`worker/game-variant.ts:238` **main**).
  When it failed, the script carried on and installed and enabled a unit
  around a container that did not exist. systemd then restarted that unit
  forever (85 times).
- **Nothing to re-run.** Cloud-init runs the snippet once per instance. A
  retry does not reboot the guest, so attempts 2 and 3 had no mechanism at all
  to re-run the setup. They waited 300 s for a port that nothing would ever
  open.

### Root cause 3: credentials rotated on retry

`provision()` minted a **new management keypair on every attempt**
(`worker/index.ts:1031` **main**), stored it, and put it in `sshkeys`
(`worker/index.ts:1044` **main**). Cloud-init installs `sshkeys` on the first
boot only, so from attempt 2 on the DB held a key the guest had never seen.

The root password was already handled correctly
(`worker/index.ts:759` **main**, fixed 2026-08-28): it is reused when a vmid
exists. The key never got the same treatment. In this incident the duplicate
IP masked the effect, but on a correctly addressed VM it still breaks every
key-based login (control panel, mods, backups) after any retried provision.

### Contributing: non-primary node first boot

- **Shared Docker Hub budget.** node-2 is a NAT island. Every VM there shares
  one public egress IP, and so one anonymous Docker Hub pull budget. Every
  provision, reinstall and sweep on that node pulls from Docker Hub directly.
  There is no mirror or cache, and game images are not pinned by digest.
- **Hidden probe errors.** `waitOutGameInstall` gave up on the first failed
  probe and discarded the error message.

---

## What changed (this branch)

### 1. IPAM knows what the node knows

- **Inventory.** `lib/node-ip-inventory.ts` reads every qemu and LXC config on
  the node. `lib/provision-guard.ts` parses `ipconfigN ip=` and LXC `netN ip=`
  plus MACs (`ipsFromVmConfig`, `macsFromVmConfig`). The live ARP table comes
  from the worker's own `ip -4 -j neigh` on the primary, or from the new
  read-only node-agent endpoint `GET /v1/net/neigh` (agent v4,
  `node-agent/index.js`) elsewhere.
- **Allocation.** `allocateIp(nodeId, serverId, { heldElsewhere })`
  (`lib/ipam.ts`) excludes every address held by another VM or answering ARP
  from a foreign MAC.
- **Retries re-prove their address.** `provision()` checks the address already
  on the row with `ipConflictReason`. A conflict throws `ProvisionStopError`,
  which fails at once, names the other VMs, and never touches them.
- **Fail loudly.** If the VM configs cannot be read, the provision stops. It
  never guesses. The emergency switch `NXEON_IP_INVENTORY=off` restores the
  old DB-only behaviour.
- **Fleet audit.** `worker/ip-audit.ts` runs at start-up and every 6 h as the
  `fleet-ip-audit` sweep. It is **report-only** and logs each finding to
  ErrorLog under `fleet.ip-audit`:
  - duplicate IPs,
  - DB rows whose IP differs from their own VM config,
  - DB rows whose IP is also configured on another VM.

  `scripts/fleet-ip-audit.ts` runs the same audit on demand.

### 2. Log in with what the guest has, and prove it is the right guest

All in `provision()`, after the SSH banner check. Helpers are in
`worker/provision-guest.ts`.

- **Login** (`ensureGuestAccess`): log in with the stored credentials only
  (management key, then password), using up to 4 plain attempts so first-boot
  cloud-init has time to finish. On an authentication failure, re-apply the
  same stored password through the QEMU guest agent (`applyPasswordToGuest`,
  addressed by vmid) and try again. If the guest still rejects it, the reason
  says the SSH address reaches a different machine (`ProvisionStopError`).
- **Identity** (`verifyGuestIdentity`): compare
  `/sys/class/dmi/id/product_uuid` with the VM config's `smbios1 uuid=`, with
  the hostname as a fallback. A mismatch stops the provision before anything
  is run or written.
- **Key install.** Only after identity passes, `installManagementKey`
  idempotently appends the stored public key (passed on STDIN).
- **No rotation.** The management key is reused once a vmid exists
  (`shouldReuseManagementKey`).

`NXEON_PROVISION_GUEST_CHECKS=0` disables this whole block.

### 3. Game setup is retried, idempotent, resumable and observable

`wrapDockerGameService` (`worker/game-variant.ts`), the single place every
family's `docker run -d` is rewritten:

- **Retried create.** `docker create` (which does the pull) is retried up to
  `CREATE_ATTEMPTS = 6` times with 15/30/45/60/75 s backoff. Layers that
  finished downloading are kept by dockerd, so a retry resumes.
- **Idempotent.** An existing container built from the same command (a
  SHA-256 prefix stored in `/var/lib/nxeon/game-container.cfg`) is kept. A
  container built from a different command, such as an earlier attempt's
  broken config, is replaced. A re-run therefore re-applies a corrected
  config.
- **Observable.** Progress and failures go to
  `/var/lib/nxeon/game-setup.state`. The setup PID is in
  `/var/lib/nxeon/game-setup.pid`, and `flock` prevents two runs overlapping.
- **Unit backoff.** The unit adds `RestartSteps=5` and `RestartMaxDelaySec=120`
  (restarts back off from 5 s to 120 s; systemd ≥ 254 is needed, older
  versions ignore the keys) and `StartLimitIntervalSec=0` (a customer's
  Start/Restart is never refused). `Restart=always` is kept on purpose: an
  in-game `/stop` that exits 0 must keep its current power semantics, which R
  owns.
- **Retried docker install.** `get.docker.com` is retried 3 times.
- **Registry mirror.** `NXEON_DOCKER_REGISTRY_MIRROR` (opt-in, validated)
  writes `daemon.json` `registry-mirrors` on a guest that has no Docker yet.

Cloud-init now starts the setup as its own transient unit
(`systemd-run --unit=nxeon-setup`, `worker/cloud-init-parts.ts`), with the old
nohup as a fallback.

### 4. Readiness uses the guest's evidence

- **Startup verdicts.** `classifyStartup` (`lib/provision-guard.ts`) takes one
  sample from `startupProbeCommand`: unit NRestarts, container state, exit
  code, last run length, setup state, whether setup is still running, and the
  unit journal, docker logs and setup log tails. It returns `wait`, `repair`
  or `fatal`.
- **When it runs.** Before the port wait, every third port attempt (about
  every 30 s, through `shouldAbort` in `retryCheck`/`checkGamePortOpen`), and
  on every extended-wait sample.
- **`fatal`** means the game exits on start: 2 restarts with a recognised
  fatal line, or 3 without one, counted from the start of the wait. The
  provision ends immediately. `Job.error`'s first line is customer-safe, and
  the following lines carry the game's own last lines with secrets redacted
  (`formatGuestLines`). With a recognised line it is a `ProvisionStopError`
  (no retry). A bare restart loop keeps the normal retry path.
- **`repair`** means no container and no setup running. The worker writes a
  fresh copy of the game setup via STDIN to `/root/nxeon-game-setup.sh` and
  launches it detached (`relaunchGameSetup`). It then keeps polling with
  short reads, once per attempt. If it is still broken, the attempt fails with
  the setup's own output.
- **Retry on a booted guest.** It always re-applies the current config through
  the setup before waiting. Cloud-init will not run again.
- **`waitOutGameInstall`** tolerates 2 failed probes, gives up on the third,
  and reports the real error.
- **No retry for deterministic failures.** `runJob` fails a `ProvisionStopError`
  immediately instead of using up the remaining attempts.

### 5. Blank identity values

- PZ `ADMIN_USERNAME` now defaults to `"admin"` (`lib/game-config.ts`).
- `applyGameConfigEnv` never substitutes a blank identity value
  (`isIdentityEnvKey`) over a non-blank catalog one.
- `provision()` persists `blankIdentityDefaults(...)` (the catalog value, or
  `"admin"`) into `gameConfig` alongside the minted secrets, so the customer
  sees the real admin user in Settings.

### 6. Self-check

`scripts/verify-game-provision.ts <serverId|hostname> [--json]` is read-only.
It checks:

- VM running,
- private IP not configured elsewhere on the node,
- identity,
- container running,
- setup state,
- recent fatal lines,
- unit active with no automatic restarts in the last 10 min,
- image and digest,
- disk,
- memory vs plan, including Proxmox memory and balloon,
- every join port bound in the guest,
- every join port reachable from outside (TCP connect, or A2S for UDP).

It exits 0 only with `CLEAN BILL OF HEALTH`.

---

## Design only: registry mirror / pull-through cache for non-primary nodes

The opt-in hook is built (`NXEON_DOCKER_REGISTRY_MIRROR`). The cache itself is
not.

1. **Where.** Run `registry:2` in proxy mode
   (`REGISTRY_PROXY_REMOTEURL=https://registry-1.docker.io`, ideally with a
   Docker Hub account token so the cache pulls with authenticated limits) on
   each node's host, listening only on the NAT bridge gateway
   (`10.20.N.1:5000`). Guests reach it without leaving the node, and the node
   pulls each layer once for all its VMs. A single cache on the primary would
   force non-primary guests across the public internet to the primary. That
   is slower than Docker Hub's CDN, so a per-node cache is preferred.
2. **How guests use it.** Set the mirror per node rather than globally: store
   it on `Node` (e.g. `Node.registryMirror`). A global env var is the stop-gap.
   Docker falls back to the upstream registry when the mirror fails, so a dead
   cache costs nothing.
3. **Pre-warm.** After a catalog image changes, pull every catalog image
   through each node's cache.
4. **Digest pinning.** The platform does not record image digests today. The
   catalog uses tags, and Minecraft is the only family with a pinned artifact
   (the jar mirror). Recording `RepoDigests` after a verified provision
   (`scripts/verify-game-provision.ts` prints it) and pinning `image@sha256:…`
   in the catalog would make every node pull the identical, cache-friendly
   image. It is not done here because it changes the catalog contract, which
   D2 owns.

## Residual risks / not verified

- **No live run.** Per this task's rules, nothing was run against a real node
  or VM. The generated setup was executed against a fake `docker` in a temp
  dir (`test/provision-first-boot.test.ts`). The SSH, guest-agent and Proxmox
  paths are tested with fakes only.
- **Proxmox token permissions.** Every provision now reads every VM config on
  its node, which needs `VM.Audit` on `/vms`. If any node's token lacks it,
  provisions on that node stop with a clear error. Check first with
  `npx tsx scripts/fleet-ip-audit.ts`: an `unreadable` line identifies the
  node.
- **ARP on non-primary nodes** needs node-agent v4, which must be redeployed
  to each node. Until then those nodes are checked against VM configs only.
  This is logged, not fatal.
- **Restart backoff** applies only to units written by new provisions and
  reinstalls. Existing servers keep their current unit.
- **Unrelated failing tests.** 17 test files fail on `main` before and after
  this change (pricing, proration, auth-lockouts and others); they are not
  related to this work.

/opt/nxeon-wt-provfix
## Provisioning pipeline, timings and golden templates

What a `PROVISION` job actually does, where the time goes, and how to make it faster. Measured
2026-10-01 (prod `Job` table + `journalctl -u nxeon-worker` + Proxmox task logs + three timed test
clones on node-5/node-2). Code: `provision()` in `worker/index.ts`, `lib/golden-template.ts`,
`worker/cloud-init-parts.ts`, `worker/game-variant.ts`, `scripts/golden/`.

### The pipeline, in order

| # | Step | Where | Typical time |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Queue wait (job `createdAt` → worker picks it up) | worker loop | 0-40s; up to 137s observed while the worker ran 1 job at a time (now `WORKER_CONCURRENCY=8`) |
| 2 | vmid (never-reuse floor), dedicated IP / NAT IP + SSH port, password, DB writes | `allocateFreshVmid`, `lib/ipam.ts` | 1-2s |
| 3 | `qm clone` (full copy) of `OsTemplate.baseVmid` — or a golden template | Proxmox | 4s (node-5 NVMe, stock 3.5 GB) · 24.5s (node-2, stock) · 67.7s (node-2, 4.2 GB golden, full) · **2.1s (node-2, golden, linked)** |
| 4 | Per-VM cloud-init snippet (primary: local file, others: node-agent) + config + resize | Proxmox | ~3s |
| 5 | NAT forward sync (all 5 nodes) | `worker/network.ts` | ~2s |
| 6 | Start | Proxmox | ~1s |
| 7 | Guest-agent wait | `waitForGuestAgent` | was **a fixed 180s on every provision** (bug, see below); now = real boot: ~15s golden, ~90-120s stock |
| 8 | SSH reachability (banner) | `checkSshReachable`, 5s interval | ~15-20s after start |
| 9 | Game port (TCP connect, or UDP + in-guest bound socket) | `checkGamePortOpen` 300s, then `waitOutGameInstall` up to 45 min while the guest shows progress | depends on the game (below) |
| 10 | RUNNING, emails, join-port forwards, admin-port retraction, `SYNC_GAME_DNS`, optional `GAME_CONFIG` | `provision()` tail | ~5s |

Inside the guest (stock Ubuntu 24.04, 2 vCPU / 2 GB, measured on node-5):

| Phase | Time after start |
|---|---|
| sshd answers (key auth) | 23s |
| cloud-init `package_update` + `qemu-guest-agent` + `unzip` | **72.2s** (`config-package_update_upgrade_install`) |
| guest agent up / runcmd starts | 95s |
| Claude CLI install (used to run BEFORE the game) | +10s |
| `get.docker.com` + `itzg/minecraft-server:java21` pull + `docker create` | +25s (stock) · +1.2s (golden) |
| Minecraft world generation → port 25565 open | +30-35s |

## Troubleshooting — provisioning and the worker

| Symptom | Cause | Fix / where to look |
|---|---|---|
| Button does nothing, no error | One in-flight job per server; a `RUNNING` row blocks every later action | Queue-check SQL in the restart runbook; a worker restart trips `reapStuckJobs` |
| SSL "stuck pending" for many minutes | The worker is a **strictly serial** single-job queue; the cert is behind a long job. One cert sat `PENDING` 13m15s behind a 24-minute migration | Not a bug, a design limit. Queue position is resolved at `app/dashboard/ssl/page.tsx:44` |
| Server stuck `PROVISIONING`/`REINSTALLING`/`DELETING` | Worker died mid-job | `reapStuckJobs()` `worker/index.ts:1113` requeues under 3 attempts, else `ERROR` + reconcile |
| A backup shut the server down | `BACKUP_CREATE` was treated as a VM-state failure | **Fixed** — excluded from `VM_STATE_FAILURE_JOBS` (`worker/index.ts:50-53`); backups use `mode: "snapshot"`. A failed backup now notifies on its final attempt (`:861-872`) instead of being silent |
| A failed disk expansion marked the server `ERROR` | `DISK_EXPAND` was in the failure set | **Fixed** — deliberately absent (`worker/index.ts:44`); money unwound by `reconcileFailedDiskExpand` (`:822`) |
| Customer holds extra disk; a plan resize hard-fails | Resize computed the target as `plan.diskGB`, i.e. a *shrink* | **Fixed** — worker resizes to `plan.diskGB + extraDiskGB` (`worker/index.ts:559`) |
| Reinstall wiped an attached volume | No guard | **Fixed** — `worker/index.ts:428-448`, `lib/actions.ts:464-471` |

  published => unmet), `archive` (strict `lib/mods/archive.ts` read with every entry inflated: links,

  node; one at a time; QA account `qa-sweep@nxeon-internal.test`, hostnames `qa-modverify-*`; real
  `placeGameOrder` -> PROVISION, `enqueueModOp` install, `GAME_POWER` restart, `readGameLogs`, DELETE job in
